unit.name: Earth Through Time and Across the Solar System
unit.subtitle: Track climate, sea level and atmospheric change on Earth and use other planets as analogues

lessons.title: Icehouse and Greenhouse Earth
lessons.description: Rock evidence for Earth's major swings between frozen icehouse and warm greenhouse states.
lessons.content_html:
A Planet That Has Changed Its Mind

Earth’s climate has never been fixed. Over hundreds of millions of years, the planet has swung between two extremes: icehouse conditions — when ice sheets spread across the continents — and greenhouse conditions — when the planet was so warm that ice barely existed even at the poles. These dramatic shifts are recorded in the rock record, and geologists read them like the pages of a climate history book.

Understanding past climate states is one of the most powerful tools in geology. If you know the conditions under which a rock formed, you can reconstruct where on Earth that area sat, what the sea level was doing, and how the atmosphere was behaving at the time. This lesson focuses on the two key states and the rocks that provide the evidence for each.

Key Fact

Tillite is the key rock evidence for icehouse conditions. It is lithified (solidified) glacial till — a jumbled, poorly sorted mixture of sand, pebbles and boulders dropped directly by ice. Finding tillite in a region tells geologists that glaciers once covered that area, even if the region sits in the tropics today.

Icehouse Earth: Evidence from Tillites

The Carboniferous and Permian periods (roughly 360–250 million years ago) represent a major icehouse phase. At that time, the supercontinent Gondwana sat over the South Pole, and enormous glaciers spread across what is now South America, Africa, Antarctica, India and Australia. As these continents drifted northward over geological time, the tillites they carried moved with them. Today, Carboniferous tillites are found in South America and southern Africa — regions that are now tropical or temperate, far from any ice.

Tillites are identified by several features that distinguish them from other poorly sorted rocks. The fragments are angular rather than rounded, showing they were not transported by water (which rounds particles). They show no layering or grading because glaciers dump all particle sizes together without any sorting. Striated (scratched) pebbles and polished bedrock surfaces beneath tillites are further evidence that ice dragged rocks across the landscape. In your exam, identifying tillite as evidence of glaciation — and explaining why its poor sorting and angular clasts indicate a glacial origin — is a high-value skill.

Students sometimes confuse tillite with other poorly sorted sedimentary rocks such as conglomerate or breccia. The key differences are: (1) conglomerates contain rounded clasts (water-transported), whereas tillite clasts are angular; (2) breccias have angular clasts but typically show better sorting and are deposited by gravity flows (screes, landslides), not by ice; (3) tillite contains a chaotic mixture of clay, sand and boulders with no grading or layering — a signature of direct glacial deposition. Striated surfaces on individual clasts are unique to glacial environments and are the clinching piece of evidence.

Greenhouse Earth: Evidence from Limestones and Chalk

Greenhouse conditions are recorded by a very different set of rocks. When global temperatures were high and ice was absent, sea levels rose because no water was locked in polar ice sheets. Warm, shallow seas spread across low-lying continental areas. In these conditions, limestone accumulated as marine organisms such as corals, brachiopods and crinoids built their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate dissolved in the warm water.

The British area provides a compelling record of these greenhouse phases. During the Carboniferous period (before the full glaciation of Gondwana reached its maximum), warm tropical seas covered much of Britain, depositing the Carboniferous Limestone that forms the Yorkshire Dales, the Mendips and the Peak District today. Fossil corals found in these rocks — species that only live in warm, shallow tropical water — confirm that Britain sat near the equator at the time, in greenhouse-like conditions.

Key Fact

Chalk is a pure white limestone made almost entirely of the microscopic remains of coccolithophores — tiny floating algae. Chalk formed during the Cretaceous period (roughly 145–66 million years ago), a profound greenhouse phase when global temperatures were 6–10°C warmer than today and sea levels were 100–200 m higher than at present. The White Cliffs of Dover, the North and South Downs, and the Yorkshire Wolds are all made of Cretaceous Chalk.

Latitude Change and the British Record

One of the most important insights from comparing icehouse and greenhouse rocks in Britain is that the rock type alone is not enough — latitude change through plate movement must be considered too. Britain has drifted northward over geological time. During the Lower Palaeozoic (Cambrian to Devonian, roughly 540–360 million years ago), what is now Britain sat in the southern hemisphere tropics or subtropics, so warm-water carbonates and reef limestones are found in Wales and Scotland from this era.

By the Cenozoic (66 million years ago to the present), Britain had reached its current mid-latitude position. The most recent icehouse phase — the Pleistocene glaciations, beginning about 2.6 million years ago — left behind boulder clays, drumlins and glacial erratics across Scotland, northern England and Wales. These form the youngest glacial record in the British sequence and sit directly above older greenhouse-phase sediments, dramatically illustrating how climate and plate position have both changed over deep time.

Students often assume that if a tropical rock (such as reef limestone) is found in Scotland, it simply means Scotland was once warm. This conflates two separate factors. Latitude change through plate tectonics is one driver — Scotland was once near the equator. But global climate state matters too: during a full greenhouse phase, even mid-latitude areas have warm climates, whereas during an icehouse phase, even equatorial regions can be cooler than today’s tropics. A complete exam answer distinguishes between these two effects and addresses both when interpreting British rock sequences.

Reading the Rock Record as a Climate Archive

The value of the icehouse–greenhouse framework is that it connects rock type, fossil content, latitude history, and global sea level into a single coherent narrative. Tillites tell you ice was present; limestones and chalk tell you warm, shallow seas prevailed. Together, they reveal that Earth has experienced multiple icehouse and greenhouse phases through its 4.54-billion-year history — and that the planet’s climate is capable of extreme swings on timescales of tens of millions of years.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to identify evidence for an icehouse or greenhouse period, name the rock type and then explain what feature of it proves the climate interpretation — for tillite, it is the poor sorting, angular clasts and striated surfaces; for limestone or chalk, it is the warm-water marine fossils and the conditions required for calcium carbonate to accumulate. Simply naming the rock without explaining the evidence will not earn full marks. If the question asks you to compare icehouse and greenhouse conditions, you must address both in each point you make — for example “icehouse rocks are tillites with angular unsorted clasts, whereas greenhouse rocks are limestones formed from warm-water marine organisms.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Icehouse conditions are evidenced by tillites — poorly sorted, angular, unsorted glacial deposits that record the presence of continental ice sheets, such as Carboniferous tillites in South America and Africa.
  • Greenhouse conditions are evidenced by limestones (including chalk) — warm-water carbonate rocks formed in shallow seas when global temperatures were high and ice was absent, such as Cretaceous Chalk across southern England.
  • Both latitude change through plate tectonics and global climate state must be considered when interpreting past rock sequences in Britain — the two factors act together and must not be confused.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following rock types provides the best evidence for a past icehouse period?
A) Oolitic limestone
B) Chalk
C) Tillite
D) Coal
practice_questions.marks: C) Tillite [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one feature of tillite that distinguishes it from a water-deposited conglomerate.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any of: angular (not rounded) clasts / poorly sorted with no grading / chaotic mix of clay, sand and boulders / presence of striated clasts [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how chalk forms and what climate conditions its presence indicates.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for describing formation (accumulated from microscopic coccolithophore remains / calcium carbonate microfossils settling on the seafloor in warm shallow seas). One mark for climate indication (greenhouse conditions / high global temperatures / sea level significantly higher than today / absence of polar ice) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why Carboniferous tillites are found in South America and Africa today, even though those regions are now tropical.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that during the Carboniferous, South America and Africa were part of Gondwana, which sat over the South Pole; plate tectonics has since moved these landmasses to lower latitudes, carrying the tillites with them; therefore the present-day latitude of the rock does not reflect the latitude at which it was deposited.
Secure: Identifies Gondwana over the South Pole and plate movement northward, but explanation of the mismatch between present and past latitude is less fully developed.
Developing: States that the landmasses used to be at higher latitudes / further south, without clearly linking to Gondwana or plate tectonics.
Emerging: States that it was cold in the past without explaining plate movement. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A geologist finds a sequence of rocks in Wales that includes Carboniferous Limestone overlain by Carboniferous tillite. Explain what this sequence tells us about the change in climate during the Carboniferous period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the limestone below indicates earlier warm, shallow marine greenhouse conditions; the tillite above indicates a shift to icehouse conditions with glaciation; cross-cutting relationships show the change was from warmer to colder, linking to the southward position of Gondwana and the growth of polar ice sheets.
Secure: Identifies both rock types and links each to greenhouse/icehouse conditions; explains the sequence as a climate cooling event.
Developing: Identifies one rock type correctly with the correct climate; does not fully develop the change or the sequence.
Emerging: States that the sequence shows climate change without linking rock types to conditions. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively the rock record can be used to reconstruct past climate states on Earth. In your answer, refer to specific rock types and the evidence they provide.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates the rock record as a powerful but incomplete climate archive. Strengths: tillites provide unambiguous evidence of past glaciation (poor sorting, angular clasts, striated surfaces); limestones and chalk record warm shallow marine conditions (warm-water fossils, high sea level); the sequence of rock types through time allows climate changes to be detected. Limitations: plate tectonic movement means rock latitude must be corrected before climate interpretation; some rock types (e.g. coal) form under a range of conditions and are less diagnostic; erosion removes parts of the record. Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Covers at least two rock types with specific evidence, addresses one strength and one limitation, reaches a conclusion.
Developing: Describes rock types and their climate association but does not evaluate or discuss limitations.
Emerging: Makes simple points about climate change in rock record without specific rock evidence. [6 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: A prolonged period of Earth history when global temperatures were low, ice sheets covered large parts of the continents, and sea levels were reduced.
A prolonged period of Earth history when global temperatures were high, polar ice was absent or minimal, and warm shallow seas covered much of the land.
A sedimentary rock made of poorly sorted angular fragments of all sizes, deposited directly by glaciers without the sorting action of water or wind.
A sedimentary rock composed chiefly of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), often formed from the remains of marine organisms such as corals, shells and microfossils in warm shallow seas.
Microscopic planktonic algae with calcium carbonate plates (coccoliths) that floated in warm Cretaceous seas and settled to form chalk after death.

lessons.title: Sea Level Change and Drowned Forests
lessons.description: How ice sheet growth and melting drive global sea level change, with drowned forest evidence.
lessons.content_html:
Why Does the Sea Rise and Fall?

Sea level is not fixed. Over geological time, it has risen and fallen by hundreds of metres — and those changes have left striking evidence in the geological record. The primary control on global sea level is how much water is stored as ice. When continental ice sheets grow, they lock up vast amounts of water as solid ice, and sea levels around the world fall. When those ice sheets melt, the water returns to the oceans and sea levels rise. This is eustatic sea level change — a global shift driven by changes in ocean water volume.

Understanding the link between ice and sea level is central to this unit. It connects the icehouse and greenhouse climate states you studied in the previous lesson directly to the landscape evidence we can see on coastlines and on the seabed today. Examiners regularly ask students to explain the mechanism behind sea level change, so mastering the cause-and-effect chain is essential.

Key Fact

During an icehouse period, continental ice sheets grow by accumulating snow and ice. This locks water away from the ocean, reducing its volume. Global sea levels therefore fall — by as much as 120 metres during the peak of the last glaciation about 20,000 years ago. During warming, ice sheets melt and return water to the ocean, causing sea levels to rise.

Drowned Forests: Evidence for Rising Seas

Drowned forests are one of the most dramatic pieces of evidence for post-glacial sea level rise. Around the coasts of Britain — at places such as Borth in Wales, Redcar in Yorkshire and various beaches in Cornwall — ancient tree stumps are exposed at low tide. These are the remains of forests that grew on dry land thousands of years ago, during and after the last glaciation when sea levels were much lower than today.

As the ice sheets of the last glaciation melted (beginning around 18,000 years ago), meltwater flooded back into the ocean and sea levels rose rapidly. The forests that had colonised low-lying coastal land were progressively submerged. Peat layers associated with the tree roots are often preserved beneath beach sediment, and radiocarbon dating of this peat confirms ages of roughly 4,000–8,000 years for many British drowned forests — showing that significant sea level rise occurred in the early Holocene after the main ice retreat.

During the peak of the last glaciation, sea levels were roughly 120 metres lower than today and a large area of dry land connected Britain to mainland Europe across what is now the southern North Sea. Geologists call this area Doggerland. It was a landscape of rivers, lakes and forests, inhabited by early humans. As the Pleistocene ice sheets melted during the Holocene, sea levels rose and Doggerland was progressively flooded. By about 6,500 years ago, Britain had become an island. Trawler nets in the North Sea occasionally dredge up worked flint tools and animal bones, confirming the former existence of this inhabited landscape beneath the sea.

The Scale of Ice: How Much Sea Level Change?

The size of an ice sheet determines how much sea level falls when it forms. The larger the ice extent, the more water is removed from the oceans. During the Last Glacial Maximum around 20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America, Scandinavia, and Britain north of the Thames–Severn line. Global sea levels were approximately 120 metres below their current level. Conversely, if the current Antarctic ice sheet were to melt completely, sea levels would rise by approximately 58 metres — enough to flood all coastal cities on Earth.

Key Fact

At the peak of the last glaciation (approximately 20,000 years ago), global sea levels were about 120 metres lower than present. This was enough to expose a land bridge between Britain and Europe (Doggerland) and to leave drowned forests along Britain’s current coastline as evidence of the lower sea level.

Global Warming, Global Cooling, and Ice Extent

The chain of causation runs in both directions. Global warming reduces ice extent by increasing melt rates. Reduced ice extent means less water stored as ice, so sea levels rise. Global cooling has the opposite effect: more snow falls than melts, ice sheets grow, water is removed from the oceans, and sea levels fall.

This process operates on a range of timescales. Orbital cycles (changes in the shape of Earth’s orbit and the tilt of its axis) drive glacial–interglacial cycles over periods of 20,000–100,000 years. Over millions of years, atmospheric carbon dioxide levels — influenced by volcanic activity and the weathering of rocks — are the dominant control on global temperature and therefore on ice volume and sea level. Both mechanisms are explored in the following lessons.

Eustatic sea level change is a global process, but local sea level change is also influenced by isostasy. When a thick ice sheet sits on a continent, its weight depresses the crust downward. When the ice melts, the crust slowly rebounds upward — a process called post-glacial isostatic rebound. In Scotland, the crust is still rising by about 1–2 mm per year because of the unloading of Pleistocene ice. This means local relative sea level in Scotland is falling even as global eustatic sea level rises. Southern England, further from the centre of ice loading, is slowly tilting downward into the North Sea. Isostasy and eustasy act simultaneously and must be distinguished in exam answers about sea level change.

Reading Sea Level Change from the Rock Record

Past sea level changes are also recorded in sedimentary sequences. When sea level rises, marine sediments (muds, sands, limestones) are deposited over formerly terrestrial or coastal deposits. When sea level falls, erosion may occur and a gap in the record — an unconformity — can result. Sequences of alternating marine and terrestrial sediments indicate repeated sea level rises and falls, and are common throughout the British Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock record.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to explain sea level change, always give the full mechanism: state whether ice is growing or melting, explain what happens to water volume in the ocean as a result, and then state the direction of sea level change. One-step answers (“sea level rose because it got warmer”) will only earn one mark. For questions involving drowned forests or Doggerland, link the evidence explicitly to post-glacial sea level rise — name the process (ice sheet melting), the direction of change (sea level rise), and explain why dry land became submerged. Watch out for questions that ask you to distinguish eustatic sea level change from isostatic (land level) change — these are tested separately.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global sea level is controlled by ice volume: growing ice sheets lock water away from the ocean, lowering sea level; melting ice sheets return water to the ocean, raising sea level. At the Last Glacial Maximum, sea levels were about 120 metres below present.
  • Drowned forests (such as those at Borth, Wales, and Redcar, Yorkshire) are exposed at low tide and provide evidence for post-glacial sea level rise as Pleistocene ice sheets melted and submerged formerly dry coastal land.
  • Eustatic (global ocean volume) changes must be distinguished from isostatic (crustal rebound) effects: Scotland is still rising as a result of post-glacial isostatic rebound, while southern England is slowly subsiding.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the cause of eustatic sea level fall?
A) The crust subsides under the weight of ice
B) More water evaporates from the ocean surface
C) Continental ice sheets grow, locking water away from the ocean
D) Ocean basins become deeper as tectonic plates move apart
practice_questions.marks: C) Continental ice sheets grow, locking water away from the ocean [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one location in Britain where a drowned forest can be observed at low tide.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any correct location, e.g. Borth (Wales) / Redcar (Yorkshire) / Cornwall coastal beaches [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the growth of a continental ice sheet leads to a fall in global sea level.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that water is removed from the ocean and stored as ice / precipitation falls as snow and accumulates. One mark for stating that this reduces the volume of water in the ocean, causing sea level to fall. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A drowned forest is found exposed on a beach at low tide. Explain what this tells geologists about past sea levels and how those sea levels changed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that trees grew on dry land when sea levels were lower than today (during the Pleistocene glaciation, when ice sheets stored large amounts of water); as the ice sheets melted at the end of the last glaciation, meltwater returned to the ocean, sea level rose progressively, and the former land surface was submerged; the preserved tree stumps now sit below the current high tide mark, proving that sea level was lower when the forest was alive.
Secure: Identifies lower past sea level (glaciation) and subsequent sea level rise (melting); two of three points developed.
Developing: States that sea level used to be lower and that the land was flooded, without linking to ice sheet changes.
Emerging: States that there used to be a forest here without explaining sea level change. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between eustatic sea level change and isostatic sea level change, using Scotland as an example of isostatic change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines eustatic as a global change in ocean water volume (driven by ice growth/melting); defines isostatic as a local change in land height relative to the sea (driven by crustal loading/unloading); applies isostasy to Scotland — the crust was depressed by Pleistocene ice and is now slowly rebounding upward as the ice is gone, so Scotland’s land surface is rising and local relative sea level is falling even as global eustatic sea level rises.
Secure: Correctly defines both terms and applies one to Scotland; all three elements present but explanation less full.
Developing: Defines one term correctly; partial application to Scotland.
Emerging: Confuses the two terms or gives only one correct point. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well drowned forests and other coastal evidence can be used to reconstruct past sea level changes. In your answer, discuss both the strengths and limitations of this type of evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strengths — drowned forests provide direct physical evidence (tree stumps, peat, radiocarbon-dateable organic material) of past land surfaces below sea level, allowing relative sea level to be quantified and dated; Doggerland evidence (flint tools from trawlers) confirms human habitation of now-submerged land. Limitations — evidence is fragmentary (wave action destroys many sites); isostatic vs eustatic contributions cannot always be separated from coastal evidence alone; relative sea level curves may differ between regions because of differential isostatic rebound; dating uncertainty. Reaches a reasoned conclusion about the value and limitations of coastal evidence.
Secure: Covers at least two strengths and one limitation with specific examples; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes drowned forests as evidence without evaluating strengths/limitations in depth.
Emerging: Simple points about sea level change without engaging with the question of how useful the evidence is. [6 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: Large masses of ice covering a substantial area of a continent, formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow over thousands of years.
A worldwide change in sea level caused by a change in the volume of water in the oceans, as opposed to local land movements.
Ancient tree stumps and root systems preserved on an intertidal beach or sea floor, exposed at low tide, showing that the area was once dry land above sea level.
A sustained increase in average global surface temperature, causing ice to melt and sea level to rise.
A sustained decrease in average global surface temperature, causing ice sheets to grow and sea level to fall.
The adjustment of the Earth's crust in response to changes in the weight placed upon it, such as the loading and unloading of ice sheets.
A surface of erosion or non-deposition that separates younger strata from older strata, representing a gap in the geological record.

lessons.title: Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide and Climate Feedbacks
lessons.description: Volcanic and fossil fuel CO2 sources, ice-core evidence, and positive and negative climate feedbacks.
lessons.content_html:
Carbon Dioxide: Earth’s Climate Thermostat

Atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) is one of the most powerful controls on global climate over geological timescales. It acts as a greenhouse gas — it allows incoming solar radiation to reach the surface but absorbs outgoing infrared radiation, warming the lower atmosphere. When CO2 concentrations are high, the planet warms; when they fall, the planet cools. Understanding where CO2 comes from, how its concentration has changed through time, and what feedback mechanisms amplify or dampen those changes is essential for GCSE Geology.

Sources of Atmospheric CO2

CO2 enters the atmosphere through two main geological pathways. The first is volcanic emissions. Volcanoes release CO2 stored in the mantle whenever magma degasses at the surface or at mid-ocean ridges. Over geological timescales of millions of years, the total rate of volcanism — controlled by how active plate tectonics is — determines the background level of atmospheric CO2. Periods of intense volcanic activity (such as the eruption of large igneous provinces like the Deccan Traps, about 66 million years ago) can significantly increase atmospheric CO2 and warm the climate.

The second pathway, operating on a much shorter human timescale, is the burning of fossil fuels. When coal, oil and natural gas are burned, carbon that was locked in rocks for hundreds of millions of years is rapidly returned to the atmosphere. The current rate of CO2 increase from fossil fuel burning is far faster than any volcanic source — approximately 100 times greater than global volcanic emissions — which is why atmospheric CO2 concentrations have risen from about 280 parts per million (ppm) before industrialisation to over 420 ppm today.

Key Fact

The two sources of atmospheric CO2 are volcanic emissions (geological timescale — millions of years) and the burning of fossil fuels (human timescale — decades to centuries). Both release carbon that was previously stored, but at very different rates. Current fossil fuel burning raises CO2 concentrations far faster than any volcanic source.

Evidence from Ice Cores

How do geologists know what atmospheric CO2 concentrations were in the past? One of the most direct pieces of evidence comes from ice cores. Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet contain air bubbles trapped when snowflakes compressed into ice hundreds of thousands of years ago. Analysing these bubbles allows scientists to measure the actual CO2 concentration of the ancient atmosphere directly. The oldest Antarctic ice cores extend back approximately 800,000 years and show that CO2 has fluctuated between roughly 180 ppm during ice ages and 280 ppm during warm interglacial periods — closely tracking global temperature as recorded by oxygen isotope ratios in the same ice.

Ice cores also contain other climate proxies. The ratio of oxygen isotopes (oxygen-18 to oxygen-16) in the ice itself records past temperature — lighter oxygen-16 evaporates preferentially from the ocean, and colder periods preserve more of it in polar ice. Dust layers in ice cores record periods of intense wind (often corresponding to cold, dry glacial episodes). Together, these proxies make ice cores one of the most information-rich climate archives available, though they only reach back 800,000 years — a tiny fraction of Earth’s history.

For periods beyond 800,000 years, geologists cannot use ice cores (no ice survives from before the Quaternary in Antarctica). Instead, they use proxy evidence from sediment cores, the carbon isotope ratios preserved in fossil shells, and the stomatal density of fossil leaves (fewer stomata open when CO2 is high). The sedimentary rock record also preserves indirect evidence — for example, the vast coal measures of the Carboniferous formed from organic carbon buried at an enormous rate, which may have drawn down CO2 and helped trigger the Carboniferous–Permian glaciation.

Positive and Negative Feedbacks

A feedback mechanism is a process that either amplifies or dampens an initial climate change. Understanding feedbacks is crucial because they determine whether a small change in CO2 leads to a small or a dramatic shift in global temperature.

A positive feedback amplifies the initial change. The ice–albedo feedback is a key example: when global temperature rises, ice melts; the dark ocean or land surface exposed has a lower albedo than ice (absorbs more radiation instead of reflecting it); this causes further warming; which melts more ice; amplifying the original warming. The water vapour feedback is similar: warming increases atmospheric water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas, causing further warming.

Key Fact

The ice–albedo positive feedback: (1) warming melts ice and snow; (2) the dark ocean or soil exposed absorbs more solar radiation than the reflective ice did; (3) this causes more warming, which melts more ice — the process reinforces itself. This is why relatively small initial changes in CO2 can lead to large shifts in global temperature.

Negative Feedbacks: Nature’s Thermostats

A negative feedback counteracts the initial change and helps stabilise the climate. The most important geological negative feedback is chemical weathering. When the climate warms, the rate of chemical weathering of silicate rocks increases (warmer temperatures and more rainfall accelerate reactions). This removes CO2 from the atmosphere (CO2 dissolves in rainwater to form carbonic acid, which reacts with silicate minerals, eventually depositing carbonate in the ocean). The reduced atmospheric CO2 then causes cooling — opposing the initial warming. Over millions of years, this “weathering thermostat” has helped prevent CO2 from rising to catastrophic levels.

Other negative feedbacks include marine storage (as CO2 rises, more dissolves in ocean water and is used by organisms to build shells, which eventually sink to the seafloor as carbonate sediment) and, over very long timescales, subduction of carbon-rich ocean crust, which returns carbon to the mantle and ultimately recycles it through volcanism over tens of millions of years. Modern engineering efforts to mimic these natural processes — known as carbon capture and sequestration — draw directly on this geological understanding.

It is easy to confuse the terms. Remember: “positive” does not mean “good” — it means the feedback amplifies the change. “Negative” does not mean “bad” — it means the feedback reduces the change and acts as a stabiliser. Exam questions often give a scenario and ask you to identify whether a feedback is positive or negative. Ask yourself: does the feedback make the initial change bigger (positive) or smaller (negative)? The ice–albedo loop makes warming bigger (positive). Chemical weathering makes warming smaller (negative). Apply that test to any scenario.

Connecting the Evidence

The ice core record, the sedimentary rock record, and our understanding of feedback mechanisms all fit together into a consistent picture: atmospheric CO2 is a powerful climate driver, but its effects are mediated by feedbacks that can either amplify small changes into major climate shifts (positive) or moderate those changes over geological time (negative). The current rapid rise in CO2 from fossil fuels is outpacing the slow negative feedbacks — particularly chemical weathering, which operates over hundreds of thousands of years — which is why human-induced climate change is proceeding faster than any natural climate cycle in the ice core record.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining a feedback, always state whether it is positive or negative first, then describe the mechanism step by step. A common error is to describe only part of the feedback loop — for example, saying “warming melts ice” without completing the loop to show how this causes further warming. For the ice–albedo feedback, you need at least three steps: warming melts ice; darker surface absorbs more radiation; more warming results. For questions on CO2 sources, be precise about the timescale: volcanic emissions are geological (millions of years), fossil fuel burning is human (decades–centuries). If a question asks about evidence for past CO2 levels, name ice cores and explain that air bubbles trap ancient atmospheric gas — do not invent proxy types.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atmospheric CO2 comes from two main sources: volcanic emissions (geological timescale) and burning of fossil fuels (human timescale). Fossil fuel burning currently raises CO2 far faster than any volcanic source.
  • Ice cores — drilled from Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets — preserve ancient air bubbles that directly record past CO2 concentrations, showing values between 180 ppm (ice ages) and 280 ppm (interglacials) over the past 800,000 years.
  • Positive feedbacks (ice–albedo, water vapour) amplify initial climate changes; negative feedbacks (chemical weathering, marine carbonate storage) oppose change and help stabilise climate over geological timescales.

glossary_terms.definition: A greenhouse gas whose concentration in the atmosphere strongly influences global temperature by trapping outgoing infrared radiation from Earth's surface.
The release of CO2 and other gases directly into the atmosphere by volcanic activity, including eruptions, fumaroles and mid-ocean ridge outgassing.
Coal, oil and natural gas formed from ancient organic material buried and transformed by heat and pressure over millions of years, which release CO2 when burned.
Cylinders of ice drilled from ice sheets such as those in Antarctica or Greenland, containing trapped air bubbles that preserve ancient atmospheric gas samples.
Cylinders of sediment drilled from ocean floors or lake beds, preserving a layered record of past environmental conditions including temperature, chemistry and biological activity.
A feedback that amplifies an initial change: the output of the system reinforces the direction of the original change, making it larger.
The fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface: snow and ice have high albedo (reflect most radiation), while dark ocean or rock surfaces have low albedo (absorb most radiation).
A feedback that dampens an initial change: the output of the system opposes the direction of the original change, stabilising the system.
The reaction of CO2 dissolved in rainwater with silicate rocks at the surface, removing CO2 from the atmosphere and depositing it as calcium carbonate in the ocean.
The process by which oceanic crust carrying carbonate sediment is pulled down into the mantle at a subduction zone, returning carbon to the mantle and eventually releasing it through volcanoes.
The deliberate removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and long-term storage in rocks, soils or the ocean to reduce greenhouse warming.

lessons.title: Planetary Geology: Earth and Its Neighbours
lessons.description: Comparing Earth, Moon and Mars: atmosphere, temperature, pressure, gravity and rock types.
lessons.content_html:
Why Compare Planets?

Geology is not confined to Earth. By studying the Moon, Mars and other bodies in the Solar System, geologists apply the same principles they use on Earth — uniformitarianism — to distant worlds. If we recognise a lava flow on Mars because it looks like basalt flows we know from Earth, we can infer the volcanic history of Mars without ever visiting it. Planetary geology uses space imagery, remote sensing data and, in some cases, physical samples (from the Moon and meteorites) to reconstruct the geological histories of other bodies and, by comparison, to better understand processes on Earth itself.

Comparing Planetary Conditions

The four bodies most directly compared in GCSE Geology are Earth, the Moon, Mars, and to a lesser extent Venus. Each has a very different combination of atmosphere, surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, and surface gravity. These differences determine what geological processes can and cannot operate on each body — and therefore what the surface geology looks like.

Earth has a substantial nitrogen–oxygen atmosphere (mean surface pressure approximately 101 kPa, or 1 atmosphere), a mean surface temperature of about 15°C, and surface gravity of 9.81 m/s2. Liquid water is stable at the surface, enabling erosion, sediment transport, and the chemical weathering that removes CO2 and moderates climate. Earth also has active plate tectonics, which recycles crust and drives volcanic activity.

The Moon has no atmosphere — its gravity (1.62 m/s2, roughly one sixth of Earth’s) is too weak to retain gas over geological time. Without an atmosphere, there is no weather, no water erosion, and no chemical weathering. Surface temperatures swing from about −170°C at night to +130°C during the day. The Moon is geologically inactive today: no plate tectonics, no active volcanism. The dominant surface processes are meteorite impact and the gradual gardening of the surface by micrometeorite bombardment. As a result, ancient features — including impact craters billions of years old — are preserved in extraordinary detail.

Key Fact

The Moon has no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics. Its dominant surface process is meteorite impact. Because there is no erosion, weathering or crustal recycling, ancient impact craters billions of years old are preserved on the lunar surface — giving geologists a record of the early Solar System bombardment history that Earth’s active geology has largely erased.

Mars: A Planet with a Geological History

Mars is a world of particular geological interest. Its atmosphere is very thin (mean surface pressure about 0.6 kPa, less than 1% of Earth’s) and composed mainly of carbon dioxide. Surface temperatures average about −60°C. Surface gravity is 3.72 m/s2 — about 38% of Earth’s. Despite these harsh conditions, Mars shows compelling geological evidence for past liquid water, including ancient river valleys, delta deposits at crater rims, and minerals such as clay minerals that only form in the presence of liquid water.

Mars also preserves the largest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, standing about 22 km above the surrounding plains and measuring about 600 km across at its base. On Earth, volcanic hot spots produce shield volcanoes (like those of Hawaii), but the Pacific Plate moves over the hot spot, so each new eruption creates a new volcano in a chain. Mars has no plate tectonics, so the lithosphere remained stationary above the hot spot for billions of years, allowing enormous amounts of lava to pile up in one place. Examiners regularly ask students to explain this difference — make sure you link Mars’s giant volcanoes to the absence of plate tectonics, not just to the size of the magma source.

Key Fact

Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km tall — nearly three times the height of Mauna Kea from its ocean base. It grew so large because Mars has no plate tectonics: the crust stayed in place over a volcanic hot spot for billions of years, allowing lava to accumulate in one location rather than being spread along a chain of smaller volcanoes as happens on Earth.

Rocks and Composition

Remote sensing and rover data confirm that Mars’s surface is dominated by basalt — the same rock type that forms Earth’s ocean floors and volcanic islands. This is consistent with a planet whose geology has been dominated by volcanic activity. The lunar highlands (pale regions of the Moon) are composed largely of anorthosite, a calcium-feldspar-rich rock that formed from a global magma ocean early in the Moon’s history. The dark lunar maria (plains) are filled with basaltic lava from later volcanic eruptions between about 3 and 1 billion years ago.

Earth’s interior structure — a solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle and crust — was determined using seismology. Information about the composition of the Solar System as a whole comes from meteorites. Chondrite meteorites in particular are thought to represent the primitive material from which the inner planets formed, giving geologists a baseline composition for the early Solar System. Comparing Earth’s crust and mantle composition with chondrite data reveals how planetary differentiation — the separation of denser iron to the core — has modified Earth’s original composition.

Uniformitarianism — the idea that “the present is the key to the past” — also extends across planets. When geologists see features on Mars that look like river deltas, braided channels or alluvial fans, they apply knowledge gained from studying the same features on Earth to interpret them as the product of flowing water. Similarly, lava flow morphology, impact ejecta patterns, and dune fields on Mars can all be interpreted using processes understood from Earth. The key limit is that conditions on Mars today are very different from Earth, so geologists must also consider the different atmospheric pressure, temperature and gravity when applying analogies. A direct copy of an Earth interpretation may be wrong if it ignores those differences.

A concise data comparison for your revision:

BodySurface gravity (m/s2)Mean surface tempAtmospheric pressure (kPa)
Earth9.81~15°C~101
Moon1.62 (~1/6 Earth)−20°C mean, large range~0 (effectively none)
Mars3.72 (~38% Earth)~−60°C~0.6 (<1% Earth)

Low gravity on the Moon means it cannot retain an atmosphere — gas molecules achieve escape velocity. Mars has a thin atmosphere partly because it also lost much of its internal heat (and therefore its magnetic field and volcanic resupply of gases) early in its history.

Planetary Geology and Earth’s History

Studying other planets helps geologists understand Earth’s own early history. The Moon and Mars have preserved their ancient surfaces because they lack Earth’s erosion and crustal recycling. By reading the bombardment history recorded in lunar and Martian craters, geologists can infer that early Earth was subjected to a similarly intense meteorite bombardment during the Hadean eon (4.6–4.0 billion years ago). Because Earth’s geological record from this era is almost entirely erased by plate tectonics and erosion, the Moon effectively acts as Earth’s early geological diary.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on planetary geology often ask you to “compare” two bodies — remember that a comparison must address both bodies in each point. Do not describe Earth alone and then Mars alone: contrast them directly. Common mistakes include listing the data (e.g. “Mars has a temperature of −60°C”) without explaining the geological consequence (e.g. “so liquid water is not stable today, meaning erosion is absent and ancient craters are preserved”). Examiners also penalise answers that say Olympus Mons is big because Mars is big — the correct answer is that Mars lacks plate tectonics, so the crust does not move away from the hot spot. If a question gives you a data table, use the specific values in your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Moon has no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics, so its dominant surface process is meteorite impact; ancient craters billions of years old are preserved, providing a record of early Solar System bombardment.
  • Mars has no plate tectonics, which explains why Olympus Mons (about 22 km tall) grew so much larger than any Earth volcano — the crust stayed fixed over the hot spot for billions of years rather than moving away as on Earth.
  • Uniformitarianism applies across planets: familiar geological processes (volcanic eruptions, river erosion, impact cratering) are identified on other worlds by their resemblance to Earth analogues, but differences in gravity, temperature and atmospheric pressure must be accounted for.

lessons.title: Impacts, Craters and Planetary History
lessons.description: How impact craters and meteorite finds inform interpretations of Earth and its biosphere.
lessons.content_html:
Craters as a Geological Tool

Every solid body in the Solar System that has a hard surface bears the scars of meteorite impacts. On the Moon and Mars, ancient craters survive for billions of years because those bodies lack the erosion and crustal recycling that erase them on Earth. On Earth, impacts have occurred throughout geological history — but most craters have been destroyed by weathering, burial, or subduction. Studying impact craters across the Solar System, and the rare well-preserved examples on Earth, reveals both the bombardment history of the inner Solar System and the profound effects that large impacts have had on the evolution of life.

Structure of an Impact Crater

When a meteorite or comet strikes a planetary surface at high velocity, it releases enormous energy in a fraction of a second. The impactor vaporises and the target rock melts, fractures and is thrown outward in all directions, forming a bowl-shaped impact crater. The key features of a typical impact crater, from largest to smallest, are:

  • The rim — a raised ring of uplifted and overturned rock surrounding the depression.
  • The ejecta blanket — a sheet of material thrown outward from the impact, covering the surrounding terrain to a depth that decreases with distance from the rim.
  • The crater floor — which may be filled with impact melt rock (solidified from the initially melted target rock) or, over time, with sediment.
  • A central peak (in larger craters) — a rebound structure formed as the initially depressed floor rebounded upward after the impact.
Key Fact

The four main features of an impact crater are: (1) the raised rim of uplifted rock; (2) the ejecta blanket of material thrown outward; (3) the crater floor, which may contain impact melt or sediment; and (4) a central peak (in large craters) formed by the elastic rebound of the crater floor. These features allow geologists to identify ancient craters even where erosion has partially degraded them.

Moon Craters and the Bombardment Record

The Moon’s surface records the full history of meteorite bombardment in the inner Solar System because it has no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics to erase craters over time. The lunar highlands — the pale, heavily cratered regions — preserve impact craters up to about 4 billion years old. The dark basaltic plains (the maria) have fewer craters because they were formed by volcanic eruptions between about 3.9 and 3.0 billion years ago, resurfacing and burying older craters.

By counting the number of craters of different sizes on a surface and applying crater counting, geologists can estimate the relative ages of different terrain units. Densely cratered regions are older; sparsely cratered regions are younger. On the Moon, the youngest recognisable features are small, fresh-looking craters with sharp rims and bright ejecta rays — features that fade over time as the surface is gardened by micrometeorites and space weathering.

Crater counting applies the principle of superposition at a planetary scale. If a small crater sits on top of an older, larger crater, the smaller one is younger. If a crater is itself heavily cratered and its rim is degraded, it is older than a nearby fresh crater with a sharp rim. This method allows geologists to build a relative time sequence for planetary surfaces without any radiometric dates — though Apollo lunar samples, radiocarbon-dated using radiometric methods, have calibrated the crater count chronology for the Moon, giving numerical ages to different crater-count densities.

Mars Craters and the Jezero Crater

Mars preserves impact craters ranging from tiny bowl-shaped depressions a few metres across to ancient multi-ring basins hundreds of kilometres in diameter. The most scientifically significant crater currently being studied is Jezero Crater, which is approximately 49 km wide. Orbital imagery reveals fan-shaped sedimentary deposits at the crater rim that are interpreted as river delta deposits — evidence that liquid water once flowed into the crater from outside, bringing sediment and potentially organic material. The Perseverance rover has been drilling rock cores from these deposits since 2021, searching for signs of past microbial life.

Jezero Crater illustrates how impact craters can function as natural traps for sediment, water and any materials carried in by rivers. On Earth, ancient impact craters that have been filled with sediment have sometimes produced economically important mineral deposits — the Sudbury Basin in Canada, for example, is a 1.85-billion-year-old impact structure that hosts one of the world’s largest nickel-copper ore deposits, thought to have formed when the impact melted and redistributed metal-rich rocks.

Key Fact

Jezero Crater on Mars is about 49 km across and contains sedimentary delta deposits at its rim, interpreted as the remains of an ancient river that flowed into the crater. NASA’s Perseverance rover landed there in February 2021 to drill cores from these deposits, which could preserve signs of ancient microbial life in the ancient lake sediments.

Impacts and the Evolution of Life on Earth

Large impacts have profoundly shaped Earth’s biosphere. The most famous example is the Chicxulub impact, which struck the Yucatan Peninsula (Mexico) about 66 million years ago. The impactor was roughly 10 km in diameter and released energy equivalent to billions of nuclear weapons. The immediate effects included wildfires, a global “impact winter” (dust and soot blocking sunlight for months to years), and the disruption of photosynthesis. The geological evidence for this event is a thin layer of iridium-enriched clay found at the Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary in rocks worldwide. Iridium is far more abundant in meteorites than in Earth’s crust, so its global spike at this boundary is interpreted as fallout from the Chicxulub impactor.

The Chicxulub event caused the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, eliminating approximately 75% of all species, including all non-avian dinosaurs. Paradoxically, it also opened ecological opportunities for the surviving mammal lineages, allowing their diversification into the forms that eventually led to primates and humans. Large impacts, while catastrophic in the short term, are therefore part of the mechanism that shaped the trajectory of biological evolution on Earth.

Earth has been struck by at least as many meteorites as the Moon, but the geological record preserves very few confirmed impact structures compared to the lunar surface. This is because Earth has: (1) active weathering and erosion by water and wind, which gradually remove crater rims and infill depressions; (2) plate tectonics, which subducts old ocean floor (where many oceanic impacts would have occurred) and drives mountain building that deforms ancient terrains; (3) abundant vegetation that covers and masks topographic features. Only about 190 confirmed impact structures are known on Earth. The Moon, with no such processes, has hundreds of thousands of craters visible to telescopes. This contrast dramatically illustrates how active geological processes on Earth erase evidence of past events that are permanently readable on quieter planetary bodies.

Reading Planetary Surfaces: Connecting the Unit

Impact craters, like all geological features, are records of events in time. The youngest craters on any planetary surface are sharp-rimmed and show unmodified ejecta; the oldest are heavily degraded or buried. By reading these features, geologists construct relative timelines for planetary bodies — the same fundamental approach used in stratigraphy on Earth. Together, the lessons in this unit have traced Earth’s climate and Solar System history through rock evidence, ice cores, sea level change, atmospheric chemistry and planetary geology, demonstrating that the geological record — on Earth and beyond — is a rich archive waiting to be decoded.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering sequence questions about impact craters, work from oldest to youngest using superposition (features that are cross-cut or buried are older) and the state of preservation (degraded rims = older; sharp rims with bright ejecta rays = younger). For questions about the Chicxulub impact and mass extinction, mention the iridium layer as the chemical evidence — this is the geological ‘fingerprint’ of the impact in the rock record worldwide. Do not confuse the impact winter (short-term dust blocking sunlight) with longer-term climate change from CO2. For Jezero Crater, the key examiner point is that the delta deposits suggest ancient liquid water, making it a target for evidence of past life.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Impact craters have a characteristic structure (raised rim, ejecta blanket, crater floor, central peak in large craters) that allows identification even in degraded form; crater counting gives relative ages of planetary surfaces.
  • Jezero Crater on Mars (~49 km across) contains ancient river delta sediments and is the site of the Perseverance rover mission (landed February 2021), investigating whether ancient life existed in the lake that once filled the crater.
  • The Chicxulub impact (~66 million years ago) caused the end-Cretaceous mass extinction; its geological evidence is a global iridium-enriched clay layer at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, a chemical signature of extraterrestrial impact.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct geological evidence for the Chicxulub impact event at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary?
A) A layer of tillite widespread across Mexico
B) A global layer of iridium-enriched clay
C) A sequence of chalk formed in warm tropical seas
D) A worldwide unconformity with no clay layer
practice_questions.marks: B) A global layer of iridium-enriched clay [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Mars crater chosen as the landing site for the Perseverance rover and state the main geological reason for its selection.
practice_questions.marks: Jezero Crater — selected because it contains sedimentary delta deposits interpreted as an ancient river flowing into the crater, suggesting the presence of past liquid water (and potentially life) [1 mark for name; accept either part alone for 1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the main structural features of an impact crater.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: raised rim of uplifted rock / ejecta blanket of ejected material / crater floor (possibly with impact melt or sediment) / central peak in large craters (rebound structure). Two marks for two clearly described features. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Moon preserves ancient impact craters billions of years old, whereas Earth has very few ancient impact structures visible at the surface.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (1) The Moon has no atmosphere, so no wind or rain erosion to degrade crater rims and fill depressions; (2) the Moon has no plate tectonics, so ancient crust is not subducted or deformed — old craters remain where they formed; (3) Earth has active weathering, erosion by water, and plate tectonics (subduction of ocean floor, mountain building) that progressively destroy and bury impact structures. All three points with clear explanation.
Secure: Two correct processes on each body clearly contrasted.
Developing: Identifies erosion or tectonics as a reason for Earth but does not fully contrast with Moon.
Emerging: States that the Moon has more craters than Earth without explaining why. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A geologist examining satellite images of the Martian surface notices that one impact crater has a sharp, well-defined rim and bright ejecta rays extending outward, while a neighbouring crater has a degraded, rounded rim and no visible ejecta. Use the principle of superposition and the state of preservation to determine the relative ages of the two craters.
practice_questions.marks: Full marks require: (1) correctly identifying the sharp-rimmed, bright-rayed crater as the younger feature and the degraded, rounded crater as the older; (2) applying superposition: older features are modified by later processes — the rounded rim has been subjected to longer exposure to space weathering and micrometeorite gardening; (3) explaining that ejecta rays fade over time as the surface is gardened, so their presence indicates youth; (4) linking to the broader principle that the least modified surface feature is youngest. [4 marks: 1 per point; maximum 4]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how evidence from impact craters on the Moon and Mars has improved our understanding of the early geological and biological history of Earth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Craters on the Moon (no erosion or recycling) give a complete bombardment record going back 4 billion years; applied to Earth via crater counting calibration using Apollo samples, this shows early Earth was intensely bombarded during the Hadean (4.6–4.0 Ga), a period almost absent from Earth's own rock record. Jezero Crater on Mars illustrates how craters trap sediment and water — river deltas inside craters preserve ancient environmental conditions including potentially biological material; the search for biosignatures there informs understanding of life's origin on Earth. The Chicxulub impact shows that large impacts reset biospheres — studying impact geology therefore informs the major extinction events in Earth's history. Evaluates the limits: planetary analogy has limits (different gravity, atmosphere, and tectonic context); absence of Mars/Moon fossils means biological conclusions are still speculative. Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Addresses at least two contributions to Earth understanding with specific examples; one limitation discussed; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes what can be learnt without clearly evaluating or reaching a conclusion.
Emerging: Makes simple points about craters or impacts without linking to Earth understanding. [6 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: A circular depression on a planetary surface formed by the hypervelocity impact of a meteorite or comet, characterised by a raised rim, ejecta blanket and, in larger craters, a central peak.
The technique of estimating the relative or absolute age of a planetary surface by counting the density of impact craters: older surfaces have more craters per unit area than younger resurfaced ones.

A principle of relative dating stating that older geological features are progressively buried or modified by younger ones; applied to planetary surfaces, impact craters formed on older terrain will themselves be cratered by later impacts.

An ancient impact crater on Mars, about 49 km in diameter, chosen as the landing site for NASA's Perseverance rover because it contains sedimentary deposits interpreted as the delta of an ancient river that flowed into the crater.

A large meteorite impact approximately 66 million years ago, recorded by a layer of iridium-enriched clay at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, linked to the mass extinction that ended the reign of non-avian dinosaurs.
A chemical element extremely rare in Earth's crust but concentrated in meteorites, used as a chemical marker for extraterrestrial impact events in the rock record.
